cross.title: Auditing AI peer reviewers: a benchmark on real scientific papers
cross.summary: LLM-based peer review is now used at production scale, but its evaluation remains limited. We introduce a benchmark that injects objective, localisable errors of four types (general issues, mathematics, numerics, citations) at three severity levels into real papers and measures each reviewer's detection rate by error type and severity, together with its false-positive rate on clean copies. We also present Skepthical, a multi-agent reviewer that verifies citation-backed claims by retrieving the cited papers, mathematics with computer algebra, and numerical claims with executed code. We apply the benchmark to two corpora of 15 recent arXiv preprints each, one in astrophysics and one in machine learning (ML), injecting a total of 357 errors, and evaluate twelve reviewer systems: six single-LLM reviewers, two Claude Code configurations, three publicly available reviewers, and Skepthical. The choice of model has the largest impact on detection rate: given the same prompt, three frontier LLMs differ by about 50 percentage points in total detection on both corpora. Tools and scaffolding help when they contribute what the model cannot supply on its own. In particular, on astrophysics, Claude Code improves on a single Claude call in mathematics and numerics detection, and enforced citation retrieval gives Skepthical the highest citation error detection rate of all systems by a large margin. This citation lead, however, is not observed on ML, where the models appear to know the literature better and Skepthical's citation detection rate is statistically indistinguishable from that of the best single LLM. False-positive rates are below 10% for most systems, but vary with prompt, model, and scaffolding, with mathematics flags the main source of false positives. The evaluation pipeline, the injected errors, and the adjudication logs are released as a benchmark.

repl.title: The Atacama Cosmology Telescope: Passband Measurements with an Analysis of Systematic Errors
repl.summary: We present measurements of the spectral response of the four Advanced ACTPol (AdvACT) multichroic detector arrays, which observed in frequency bands centered near 30, 40, 90, 150, and 220 GHz. The passbands were measured with a Fourier transform spectrometer (FTS) combined with coupling optics that direct and match the output of the FTS to the AdvACT receiver. We perform optical simulations of the FTS and coupling optics in order to model frequency-dependent systematic effects in this system, examining the systematics of each individual measurement component in detail. We use these simulations to apply corrections to the measurements and evaluate the remaining systematic uncertainty. We combine these systematic estimates with statistical errors to determine the measured passbands and their uncertainties from our FTS measurement, which are typically $0.75$ to $1.5\%$ per detector array for the central frequency. We present the passband characteristics for all measurements made by ACT in a common framework. Additionally, we discuss in detail limits set by the systematics in our measurements as well as ways to minimize the systematics of each component to improve passband measurements in the future.

repl.title: AI-Assisted Extraction of Follow-up Observations from GCN Circulars in Astro-COLIBRI
repl.summary: We present a new Astro-COLIBRI component that converts free-text GCN Circulars into structured, event-linked follow-up records and combines them with reports submitted directly by the community. A continuously running listener associates new Circulars with transient events, applies deterministic pre-analysis, and invokes a schema-constrained large language model to extract photometry, contacts, redshifts, and related metadata. The records are normalized into a common event-level database and exposed through the web and mobile interfaces as report summaries, contact tools, optical-afterglow context figures, and downloadable CSV or VOTable products. All 1,775 Circulars of an operational evaluation corpus covering the first half of 2026 completed the workflow without failures. An internal human audit of 210 Circulars found 223 of 231 assessed reports (96.5%) fully confirmed, each of the eight remaining ones containing at least one incorrect field, predominantly associated with observation timing and facility attribution. Extracted redshifts agree with three published compilations for 91.7 to 99.3% of the events they share, every disagreement tracing to a limit, a candidate-host estimate, or a later-refined value rather than to a misread Circular. The extraction also recovers 90 to 97% of the redshifts those compilations list for bursts it processed. Applied to the GCN archive since 2016, the pipeline yields 68,393 observations from 26,811 reports across 5,787 transient events, and now runs in real time on new Circulars. The reusable parsing and normalization pipeline is released as the open-source Python package astro-colibri-circular-parser.

repl.title: FAIR-Compliant Architecture for Heterogeneous Astronomical Data: KazVO Framework
repl.summary: This paper presents the architecture of the Kazakhstani National Virtual Observatory (KazVO) - an International Virtual Observatory Alliance (IVOA) compliant node that unifies the heterogeneous observational datasets of the Fesenkov Astrophysical Institute (FAI). The architectural foundation of the system is built upon a partitioned Data Lake, a German Astrophysical Virtual Observatory (GAVO) Data Center Helper Suite (DaCHS) publishing backend, and {a PostgreSQL database in which metadata for published observational products are mapped to IVOA ObsCore, while catalogs and simulation grids use dedicated relational tables}. We follow Open Science principles by introducing a metadata-only showcase model based on a four-class data embargo mechanism. Machine-to-Machine services deployed via IVOA protocols are exposed through the KazVO publishing registry registered in the global Registry of Registries (RofR), enabling analysis of Kazakhstani observational assets within external clients such as Tool for OPerations on Catalogues And Tables (TOPCAT), Aladin, and PyVO. The current implementation combines operational VO publication services and targeted photometric processing with scheduled, batch-mode data ingestion, supporting access to published historical and modern observational holdings. Replication has been validated on pilot datasets, while routine deployment at the observing sites and automated reduction of modern spectroscopic streams remain under development. The architecture provides a framework for progressively integrating these components into a complete data lifecycle.

repl.title: Model of the instrumental polarization induced by a rotating HWP with anti-reflective sub-wavelength structures for CMB polarimetry
repl.summary: Future CMB polarization experiments require precise control of instrumental systematics in the search for primordial $B$-mode polarization. A rotating half-wave plate (HWP) provides effective polarization modulation, but its non-ideal electromagnetic response can generate HWP-synchronous instrumental polarization. In this work, we characterize the response of a multi-layer sapphire HWP with anti-reflective sub-wavelength structures (SWS) using rigorous coupled-wave analysis. For three asymmetric SWS models, we find no substantial differences in the transmittance, polarization efficiency, or instrumental-polarization response that can be attributed to the type of SWS asymmetry. The fourth-harmonic instrumental polarization relevant to CMB polarization reconstruction is typically of order $10^{-4}$ in the CMB bands, which is expected to be mitigated. We further evaluate an actually fabricated SWS geometry, whose asymmetry enhances the retardance, and compare its response with that of an idealized model having the same type of asymmetry. Comparison of the realistic SWS with the idealized model shows that higher transmittance tends to be associated with lower instrumental polarization. These results suggest that improving the total transmission, including the effect of the fabricated SWS profile, may be more important for reducing HWP-induced instrumental polarization than tuning the SWS asymmetry itself.

repl.title: Benchmarking the expected performance of Bayesian parameter inference on Kilonovae
repl.summary: In the study of optical transients, parameter inference is a part of the process of extracting physical information, i.e. constraints on the source's characteristics, by comparing the observed lightcurves to the predictions of different astrophysical models and finding the model and parameter combination that make the closest match. In the developing field of the study of kilonovae (KNe), systematic uncertainties in modeling are still very large. Current-day models still struggle to fit adequately the whole multi-wavelength dataset of the AT2017gfo kilonova, associated to the Binary Neutron Star (BNS) merger GW170817, and thus obtain wide posterior distributions on the inferred source parameters. After reviewing the many sources of uncertainty embedded in KN analyses and the process of Bayesian parameter inference, we discuss how to quantify the performance of parameter inference analyses using metrics on information gain from prior to posterior. We highlight the systematic error margin hyperparameter $\sigma_{\rm sys}$, which correlates to a model's goodness-of-fit, and exhibit its major influence on Bayesian inference performance metrics. Using the example of two KN models from the literature with the Nuclear Multi-Messenger Astronomy (NMMA) Bayesian inference framework, we simulate the expected information gains that dedicated KN follow-ups with telescope networks could reasonably reach, for various observational cadences and error margins: we show that the wind ejecta's mass and electron fraction are the easiest KN parameters to constrain. We finally apply our KN analysis to the dataset of AT2017gfo to show that our information gain predictions match results on real data and discuss the complementarity of multi-messenger approaches.

repl.title: MarsRetrieval: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Planetary-Scale Geospatial Retrieval on Mars
repl.summary: Data-driven approaches like deep learning are rapidly advancing planetary science, particularly in Mars exploration. Despite recent progress, most existing benchmarks remain confined to closed-set supervised visual tasks and do not support text-guided retrieval for geospatial discovery. We introduce MarsRetrieval, a retrieval benchmark for evaluating vision-language models for Martian geospatial discovery. MarsRetrieval includes three tasks: (1) paired image-text retrieval, (2) landform retrieval, and (3) global geo-localization, covering multiple spatial scales and diverse geomorphic origins. We propose a unified retrieval-centric protocol to benchmark multimodal embedding architectures, including contrastive dual-tower encoders and generative vision-language models. Our evaluation shows MarsRetrieval is challenging: even strong foundation models often fail to capture domain-specific geomorphic distinctions. We further show that domain-specific fine-tuning is critical for generalizable geospatial discovery in planetary settings. Our code is available at this https URL

repl.title: When Should Science Act on an Interstellar Anomaly?
repl.summary: An unusual interstellar object may warrant further observation even when there is little evidence that it is artificial. The challenge is deciding which observations are worth pursuing, how much to invest in them, and when to stop. We argue that the Loeb Scale can help guide these decisions, provided its levels are understood as provisional assessments rather than estimates of the probability of extraterrestrial technology. Candidate technosignature status may justify targeted follow-up when new observations could distinguish competing explanations and the expected scientific value warrants the cost. This requires testable predictions and retrodictions, attention to natural explanations not yet considered, and recognition of the risks of false alarms. We place this argument in the broader history and philosophy of scientific anomalies and relate it to existing assessment frameworks in SETI and astrobiology. The cases of 1I/Oumuamua, 2I/Borisov, and 3I/ATLAS illustrate why classifications and research priorities must remain open to revision. Candidate status is a reason to seek better evidence while it can still be obtained, not a conclusion about an object's origin.

repl.title: HERMES: HiERarchical Modelling for Exoplanet Science
repl.summary: ESA's Ariel Space Mission will characterise the atmospheres of approximately 1000 exoplanets to quantify population-level trends. We present HERMES (HiERarchical Modelling for Exoplanet Science), a multidimensional Bayesian framework that probes population-level correlations across multiple axes of diversity. The specific use case we present is the multidimensional relation between stellar metallicity, planetary mass, and atmospheric metallicity. Starting from the Ariel Mission Candidate Sample, we select confirmed planets with available masses and stellar metallicity, inject plausible multidimensional trends and demonstrate successful parameter recovery. Simulated surveys are generated with a variety of leverage and sample size, in the presence of intrinsic astrophysical scatter and measurement noise. By fitting independent Bayesian models to each survey, we confirm that survey leverage remains a reliable predictor of trend precision even in multiple dimensions and in the presence of intrinsic astrophysical scatter. For an Ariel Tier 2 transit survey of at least 400 planets, HERMES robustly recovers the correlation between stellar and planetary metallicity despite intrinsic scatter in planetary abundances as large as 1.2 dex. These results establish HERMES as a practical tool for survey design and science yield forecasting in preparation for Ariel and other surveys probing population-level trends.

repl.title: SPLIT: Loosely-coherent inference of long-inspiral gravitational-wave sources for robustness against modeling and data outliers
repl.summary: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will detect gravitational waves (GWs) from dozens of extreme- and intermediate-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs/IMRIs). These sources will stay in-band for months to years, offering extraordinary scientific potential. However, their fully phase-coherent analysis standard in current pipelines imposes stringent waveform accuracy requirements; failing to model the signal over such long durations can result in significant systematic biases. To address this, we formulate a robust Bayesian inference framework that segments the data into blocks, infers each block coherently, and recombines the results using loosely-coherent phase information. By restricting full phase-tracking to much shorter block durations, this approach prevents significant accumulation of phase errors. We implement this methodology in \textsc{SPLIT} (Segmented Posteriors for Long-Inspiral Templates), a GPU-accelerated Python package. Applying \textsc{SPLIT} to an environment-rich injection, we demonstrate that while a fully-coherent vacuum-GR analysis incurs a maximum 1D systematic bias of $\approx 4.8\sigma$ from the truth, the shorter integration window of our loosely-coherent approach restricts such biases to $\lesssim 0.5\sigma$. Overall, despite a fractional loss of optimal signal-to-noise ratio, the substantial improvement in parameter accuracy offered by our method presents a highly advantageous trade-off for LISA and other future GW detectors.

repl.title: A comparison of particle and fluid approaches for modeling the streaming instability in global patch simulations
repl.summary: Identifying the process relevant to planet formation is still a major task. Mechanisms have been identified that can trap dust, preventing it from migrating inwards. A particular hydrodynamic instability, known as the streaming instability, is of high interest because it may be responsible for the formation of dust clumps from which the first planetesimals form. We aim to compare the outcome of non-linear streaming instability simulations using both fundamental approaches in a more realistic global disk model. The results will not be used to identify or disentangle the effect of, e.g., numerical diffusion in fluid simulations or the possibility of having crossing particle streams. Instead, they will enable us to determine whether the Lagrangian particle approach is the most suitable for numerical studies of the streaming instability. Methods: We perform 2D, axisymmetric, global, and isothermal hydrodynamic simulations using the two codes FARGO3D (dust fluid) and PLUTO (fluid, particles) to investigate the temporal evolution of dust scale height, midplane dust-to-gas ratio, and maximum dust density as well as to study velocity distributions and vorticities. For PLUTO particle simulations, we also investigate the influence of the gas Riemann solver and spatial reconstruction orders. Our results from a resolution study up to 5120 cells per gas scale height indicate convergence between PLUTO fluid and FARGO3D. Both yield a Gaussian profile dominated by small-scale, dust-depleted voids. Particle simulations with PLUTO have not yet converged, as a transient midplane dust component persists, indicating the need for even higher resolution or more particles. Using a more accurate Riemann solver or a higher-order spatial reconstruction scheme helps to bring the dust density profile closer to the converged structure.

repl.title: Millimeter-Wavelength Constraints on Circular Polarization of the Cosmic Microwave Background at Arcminute Scales with the Simons Array
repl.summary: We present constraints on the cosmic microwave background (CMB) circular polarization anisotropy at arcminute angular scales, using dedicated measurements from the Simons Array taken with a quarter-wave plate and rotating half-wave plate. A detection of circular polarization in the CMB would probe a range of proposed generation mechanisms, from Standard Model astrophysics to physics beyond it. At an observing frequency of 90 GHz, we place constraints over the multipole range $300 \leq \ell \leq 2000$, corresponding to angular scales of 5.4-36 arcmin, in bands of width $\Delta \ell = 100$, roughly tripling the highest multipole previously reached by a $V$-mode power spectrum measurement. Within this domain, we constrain the 95% confidence upper bound of $\ell (\ell+1) C_\ell^{VV} / (2\pi)$ to range from $\sim 22\,\mu\mathrm{K}_\mathrm{CMB}^2$ at the $\ell = 350$ bandpower to $\sim 3.5 \times 10^3\,\mu\mathrm{K}_\mathrm{CMB}^2$ at the $\ell = 1950$ bandpower. These limits are derived from $\sim$2.5 months of observations of each of two small regions of the sky located away from the Galactic plane, totaling $\sim$12 deg$^2$ of effective sky area. Because the methodology of this study marginalizes known foreground contamination, these bounds serve as robust, conservative limits on the true CMB circular polarization signal down to the sensitivity limits of the instrument. Additionally, we provide an experimental and analytical framework for implementing circular polarization observations on other telescopes by utilizing a quarter-wave plate and half-wave plate design.

repl.title: New Constraints on the Ultrahigh Energy Neutrino Flux from the First Array-Wide Search with the Askaryan Radio Array
repl.summary: Ultrahigh energy neutrinos ($E_\nu \gtrsim 100$ PeV) are detectable through Askaryan emission---the nanosecond-scale radio impulse emitted by relativistic particle cascades in a dielectric medium. The Askaryan Radio Array (ARA), an Askaryan detector array located at the South Pole, has been taking data for more than a decade. We present the first array-wide search for diffuse ultrahigh energy neutrinos with ARA. The search found no events on an expected background of $0.13\pm0.01\text{ (stat.)}^{+0.05}_{-0.06}\text{ (syst.)}$ events. The resulting upper limit is the most stringent from $50$ EeV to $1000$ EeV and provides the first constraints on the flux reported by the KM3NeT Collaboration that are complementary to optical Cherenkov and particle detectors. This limit also constrains UHECR source models, and excludes some models with trans-GZK proton populations at the $90\%$ confidence level. This represents the largest Askaryan detector dataset ever analyzed, demonstrating the feasibility and sensitivity of searches with large detector arrays acting as a single observatory. It also underscores the high acceptance and exposure of Askaryan detector arrays to ultrahigh energy neutrinos.

repl.title: Analysis Methodology of the Search for Ultrahigh Energy Neutrinos in 10.6 Years of Askaryan Radio Array Data
repl.summary: The Askaryan Radio Array (ARA) is an in-ice radio observatory at the South Pole designed to detect ultrahigh energy (UHE) neutrinos through Askaryan emission produced by interactions of neutrinos and their secondary particles. In this paper, we present the detailed methodology of the first array-wide search for a diffuse UHE neutrino flux using data from all five ARA stations. The dataset considered represents $10.6$ years of livetime and is three times larger than previous ARA neutrino searches. This search achieves a $28\%$ analysis efficiency for a neutrino flux corresponding to the current experimental upper limits. No neutrino candidates are observed on an expected background of $0.13\pm0.01\text{ (stat.)}^{+0.05}_{-0.06}\text{ (syst.)}$ events. We set a new upper limit on the diffuse UHE neutrino flux, which is the most stringent from $50$ EeV to $1000$ EeV. We also discuss lessons learned for future searches on large radio arrays.
